moving-to-austin-with-family-while-you-b.title: Moving with family while you build: the first year in Austin
moving-to-austin-with-family-while-you-b.description: The company landing is only half the move. Peer notes on the first family year in Austin: schools, child care, the partner's year, kids and the founder's pace.
moving-to-austin-with-family-while-you-b.html:
A founder sits near the end of the IFN meetup table, half in the conversation and half on their phone. They keep checking the time. School pickup is in an hour, and their partner has a job interview across town, so the handoff has to work. The company is doing fine: a few US customers, a small team at home, a pipeline that makes sense. The family is the part still being put together. Nobody in the house has worked out yet what a normal Tuesday looks like.

Some version of this comes up most months. This post is peer orientation on the first family year in Austin: schools and child care, the partner's year, the kids' first months, and the pace a founder can keep when the people at home need them more than usual. The First 90 days post covers housing and documents. This one is about family life, and it does not replace counsel, a doctor, or the school district.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, medical, immigration, tax, or school-admissions advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Your family's status, school eligibility, health coverage, and taxes all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

Two moves on two clocks

Founders who moved with family describe the first year as two moves happening at once. The company move has a plan. There is an entity, a bank account, a first customer, and someone to call when something breaks. The family move mostly runs on improvisation.

The company also has a team. The family has two adults, one of whom is usually busier than they expected, and children who did not choose any of this. Peers say the gap between those two moves is where most of the strain in year one comes from. The work going well does not close it. Sometimes it makes it wider, because the founder is the one person in the house with a full calendar and a reason to be out every day.

Schools: go to the district first

Parents in the room say the same thing about schools: start earlier than you think you need to, and go to the source.

Public school enrollment goes through the school district. For families living within its boundaries, Austin ISD has an enrollment page that is the place to begin. The greater Austin area includes more than one district, so peers suggest confirming which district your address belongs to before you assume anything. At the state level, the Texas Education Agency is the agency that oversees public education in Texas.

Parents' groups online are full of confident answers about enrollment. Peers say many of those answers were right for someone else's situation, or for a different year. The room does not tell anyone which documents they need, who is eligible, or when the cutoffs fall. Those questions go to the district directly, ideally in writing, so you have the answer on record.

Child care and the gap before school

Child care comes up just as often, and it is harder to plan from abroad.

Founders with younger children describe waitlists that were longer than they expected and a gap between arrival and the first day of school that nobody had budgeted time for. In that gap, one parent usually absorbs the care by default. Peers say it helps to decide out loud who that will be and for how long, instead of letting it fall on whoever is not on a sales call that morning.

The Texas Workforce Commission has a child care page with official information about child care programs in the state. Peers point to it as a starting point and then compare notes on what they actually found locally. Summer is its own problem in year one, and the parents who planned for it early say they were glad they did.

The partner's year

This is the part founders say they underestimated most.

The founder arrives with a purpose, a network that grows every week, and a reason to be in rooms like this one. The partner often arrives with a career on hold, no colleagues, and a city where they know nobody. Some partners keep remote work from home and end up living on that time zone, awake when the house is asleep. Some are starting over and job hunting in a market that does not recognize their credentials or their old employer's name.

Whether a partner can work in the US at all depends on their status. That is a question for immigration counsel, and the room does not guess at it.

What peers say helped was the partner building a life that did not run through the founder's company. Their own friends, their own groups, their own reason to leave the house. The Austin ecosystem map is written for founders, but some partners have used the community side of it to find their own way in. Partners are also welcome at the meetup as guests, and a few founders say bringing them early changed how the move felt at home.

The kids' first months

Founders talk about their children carefully in the room, and they describe what they saw instead of offering theories.

The first months at a new school can be lonely. A child may understand the lessons and still miss the jokes. Accents get noticed. Lunch looks different. Some children settle in quickly and some take most of the year. Parents mention the weekend call home, timed around the gap between Central time and wherever the grandparents live, and how a good call can leave a child cheerful or quiet for the rest of the day.

Peers do not give each other parenting advice here. When a parent is worried, the room usually says one thing: talk to the school, and if it feels like more than settling in, talk to your child's doctor or a licensed counselor. They are the right people for that question.

Guilt and the pace

The company wants everything in year one. So does the family. Founders admit there were weeks when they gave the company the better hours and the family got what was left.

Founders who look back on the first year say they wish they had decided early what was protected, before the calendar decided for them. What they named varies, but the same few things come up:

  • school drop-off or pickup on fixed days of the week
  • dinner at home most nights, even if work resumes afterward
  • one weekend day with no investor or customer calls
  • time alone with their partner, scheduled like a meeting if that is what it takes

None of this is a rule. Peers mention it because the founders who protected something had an easier second year than the ones who planned to slow down "once things settle."

Health care, early

Sort out health coverage and care early, using official sources and your own providers. Peers raise it in the first conversation and then hand it off. It is not something to piece together from the meetup table.

When we stop talking

The room is useful for patterns and for knowing you are not the only one. Bring in the right people when any of these come up:

  • Dependents' immigration status and whether a partner can work: immigration counsel
  • School eligibility, enrollment, and placement: the school district, directly
  • Health coverage for the family: a licensed insurance professional, and your own doctors for care
  • Taxes for a family that moved partway through a year: a CPA, ideally one with cross-border experience

Each of these is a separate role. Peers say the families who lined them up early had fewer surprises later in the year.

opening-an-ein-and-why-the-letter-matter.title: Opening an EIN and why the letter matters for banking
opening-an-ein-and-why-the-letter-matter.description: Why banks ask for the IRS EIN letter, where name mismatches stall applications, and how peers at IFN Austin keep the paper straight.
opening-an-ein-and-why-the-letter-matter.html:
A familiar moment at the IFN Austin meetup: a founder scrolls back through their inbox to show the table an email with a nine-digit number in it. That's their EIN. Their business bank application has been in review for two weeks, and the bank's latest message asked for "the IRS letter." They have the number but not the letter, and they aren't sure which letter the bank means. Two people across the table nod, because the same thing held up their accounts.

This is peer orientation from that room: what an EIN is, why banks care so much about the paper behind it, and where it tends to fit in the order of things. Not a filing guide. Not tax advice.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or banking advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. IRS processes, letter names, and bank requirements change, and the right answer depends on your entity, your ownership, and your status. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

What an EIN is, plainly

An Employer Identification Number is a nine-digit number the IRS assigns to a business for federal tax purposes. Plenty of companies with no employees have one, mostly because banks, payment processors, payroll providers, and larger customers ask for it before they will work with you.

The IRS explains who needs one and how to apply on its Get an Employer Identification Number page. Form SS-4 is the underlying application. The About Form SS-4 page has the current form and instructions. Peers read those directly. IRS pages change, and the source beats a forwarded screenshot.

When you have no SSN or ITIN

This is where many international founders first get stuck. The IRS online application expects the person listed as responsible for the company to have a Social Security number or ITIN, and it is only for companies whose principal place of business is in the US. A lot of people in the room had no SSN or ITIN when they formed.

The path they describe is a paper Form SS-4 sent by fax or mail, and it takes longer than the online flow. Founders whose principal place of business is outside the US also mention the IRS phone line for international applicants. The paper comes back differently too: the IRS says a fax application usually gets the number back by fax in about four business days, and mail takes about four weeks. Which channels are open, and how long each takes, changes. Peers check the IRS EIN page at the time they apply instead of relying on how someone did it last year.

Some founders hand this step to a formation service or an accountant. That can save time. Founders who go that route say one extra question up front helps: how will the IRS document itself reach you, along with the number? Founders who skipped that question often end up holding exactly what the person in the opening scene had, a number in an email.

The letter behind the number

Peers mention two documents most often.

The first is the notice the IRS issues when it assigns the number, the CP575. Depending on how you applied, it may come by mail some weeks later, or it may be available to save at the end of an online session. A few founders who applied online found that saving it was easy to miss in the moment. The IRS says the original notice cannot be duplicated, so a lost one means asking for a different document.

The second is Letter 147C, which the IRS calls "EIN Previously Assigned." Founders tend to ask for it by phone when the original notice is lost, or when a bank or processor wants confirmation that matches the company's current details. The IRS now offers a digital EIN verification notice, confusingly also named CP575, inside its Business Tax Account, and says banks accept it in place of a 147C. Not every founder can use that account. Letter names and options change, so peers check the IRS EIN page before asking.

Banks ask for this paper because they're matching records. During onboarding they compare the legal name, the EIN, and often the address against your formation documents and the IRS record. A number typed into an email from a vendor shows that someone has a number. An IRS document shows the IRS issued it to that exact entity.

Where the name match breaks

Most of the stalled applications people describe come down to small differences.

The company is "Example Labs, LLC" on the state filing and "Example Labs LLC" on the EIN notice, partly because IRS systems only accept a short list of characters in business names. Or the suffix got dropped. Or someone applied for the EIN under a trade name instead of the legal name. To a person these look identical. Some bank review processes treat them as a mismatch, and the application waits until someone sorts it out.

Responsible party issues come up too, at a higher level. The IRS expects a real individual who controls the entity to be listed. Founders have hit trouble when the person on the EIN record isn't the person opening the account, when a co-founder listed at formation has since left, or when nobody is quite sure who was entered. The IRS has a process for reporting changes (Form 8822-B, and the IRS says responsible party changes are due within 60 days). Whether you need it, and how it interacts with your ownership, is a question for a CPA, not the meetup table.

The pattern peers repeat: read the EIN document against your formation papers character by character before you start any bank or processor application. It takes a few minutes and can save weeks in a review queue.

Where it sits in the sequence

In the order most founders describe, the entity exists first, the EIN comes next, and banking comes after that. People who applied for an EIN before the state approved the final company name sometimes created the very mismatch they later had to unwind.

For more on the formation side, Forming a US company from abroad covers what peers sequence before the EIN. For the bank side, US business banking for international founders covers the rest of the document pack banks tend to request.

Where peers keep the letter

Founders who settled in smoothly usually treat company paper as its own track, separate from personal landing and from money movement. The EIN document belongs with the formation papers and governance documents, in a company folder that isn't mixed in with lease PDFs and passport scans.

Peers keep a clean digital copy and know where the original is. Some also note how and when they applied, because that context helps if they ever request a verification letter. Processors, banks, and investors can ask for the document again long after formation.

When we stop talking

Peer notes run out quickly on this topic. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • Tax classification and elections. How your entity is taxed, whether any election makes sense, and what reporting applies to a foreign-owned company. A CPA with cross-border experience is the right seat for this.
  • Responsible party questions. Who should be listed, what happens when that person changes, and how to correct the record.
  • Correcting a name or record mismatch with the IRS, especially when a bank or investor is waiting on it.
  • Complex ownership. A parent company abroad, founders in several countries, investors, or nominee arrangements. That is corporate counsel territory before anything gets filed.
  • Status questions. What your visa allows you to do inside the company is a question for immigration counsel.

raising-prices-after-years-of-underprici.title: I underpriced for years. Then I raised prices and some clients left
raising-prices-after-years-of-underprici.description: The scare is not the math. Peer notes on how underpricing starts after a move, what happened when owners raised prices, and how they told clients.
raising-prices-after-years-of-underprici.html:
An owner sits down at the IFN meetup table and says they finally did it. They raised their prices. They had put it off for a long time, rewritten the email more times than they want to admit, and then sent it on a quiet afternoon. Most clients wrote back some version of "thanks for the heads up, that's fine." Two did not. Those two were among the first clients the owner ever had in Austin, the ones who stayed when the business was small and unsure of itself. Both said they would look elsewhere. The owner feels relieved and a little sick, both at once, and wants to know whether they got it wrong.

The room hears some version of this most months, and people have strong opinions about it. The math tends to be the easy part. The hard part is pressing send and then waiting to see who stays. This post is peer orientation on how underpricing tends to start for founders who moved here, what peers say happened after they raised, and how they handled the conversation. It does not tell you what to charge, and it does not replace an accountant, a CPA, or counsel.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, or financial advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Contract terms, sales tax, and whether your pricing supports your business all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

How the low price got there

Few founders in the room set a low price on purpose. It crept in, usually for reasons that made sense at the time.

Home-market numbers. Some owners carried over prices that worked at home, sometimes converted and sometimes not, and never went back to check them against what the same work costs to deliver here. Rent, insurance, software and their own time can cost more here than the old price assumed.

Pricing to win the first US customers. With no local references and no network, a low number felt like the only way to get a yes. That first yes mattered. But the number that won it became the reference point for every client after.

A discount that became the price. One client got a break during a slow stretch. They mentioned it to a friend. The friend asked for the same. A year later nobody remembers it was ever a discount.

Feeling like a newcomer who has to earn it. This one gets the most nods. Many founders who came from somewhere else describe a habit of being grateful for any client at all. Every yes feels like a favor, and charging a full rate feels like asking for something you have not earned yet. Peers say this habit outlasts the business reasons. The client list grows, the references pile up, and the price stays where it was because raising it still feels presumptuous.

If you are earlier than this and still deciding how to price before you land, the validation post covers how peers test demand before a number hardens.

What happened after peers raised

Nobody in the room claims raising prices is free of risk. Some clients leave. What founders describe is more mixed than the fear they carried beforehand.

The clients who left were often the ones who were already the hardest to work with. They pushed scope, paid late, or asked for one more round of revisions every time. Owners say they did not fully see how much those clients cost them until they were gone. Not every departure fits that pattern, though. Sometimes a good, loyal client leaves because their own budget is tight, and that one stings for a while.

The work usually got lighter. Fewer clients at a fair rate left room to do better work for the ones who stayed, or to take on new ones without burning out. Several founders say they did not realize how tired they were until that pressure eased.

Some clients came back. A few tried a cheaper option, found it did not fit, and returned, sometimes a little sheepish about it. Others never came back, and the owner made peace with that.

New clients who never knew the old price mostly did not react at all. To them it was just the price.

How peers went about it

The room does not pass around scripts, and this is not the place for one. What comes up again and again is a handful of habits.

Peers gave notice. They picked a date some weeks out instead of making the change effective right away, so clients had time to plan and budget. If you have written agreements, check what they say about notice and price changes before you pick a date. That is a question for counsel.

They told their regulars first, in person or on a call, before any email went out. Owners say this was the conversation they dreaded most, and also the one that went best. A long-time client who hears it from you directly tends to take it differently than one who finds it in an inbox.

They were plain about why: costs went up, the work grew, the old number no longer reflected what they deliver. A sentence or two was enough.

And they tried not to over-explain. This is where the room gets most animated. Founders who wrote long, apologetic messages full of justification say they got more pushback and more requests to negotiate. The apology signaled the price was open for discussion. A short, warm, clear message landed better.

The room is split on grace periods for long-time clients. Some owners kept a few regulars at the old rate for a while as thanks. Others say that just delayed the same conversation. Fuller wording examples live with membership.

If you sell a product rather than a service, the conversation shifts toward packaging and tiers, which the go-to-market post covers.

The feelings that come with it

Guilt comes up first. Owners feel they are letting down the people who believed in them early. Peers in the room tend to push back gently: a business that cannot sustain itself does not serve those early clients well either.

Then the small-community fear. Many founders in the room built their first client base through their own community: the same cultural association, the same place of worship, friends of friends. When clients are also neighbors, raising prices can feel like a social risk as much as a business one, and the worry is that everyone will hear and think less of you. Founders who went through it mostly say fewer people heard than they feared, and some who did hear respected the decision.

Then the quiet voice that says you are not worth it yet. Peers say waiting does not make it go away. It got quieter for them only after the email went out and the business was still standing. If the stress of it all starts to feel heavier than a pricing decision should, talking it through with a doctor, therapist or counselor is a reasonable step, separate from anything the room can offer.

When we stop talking

The room is useful for patterns and for hearing that others have been through it. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • Contract terms, notice clauses, and whether you can change prices during an existing agreement: counsel
  • Sales tax on what you sell, and how a price change shows up on invoices and filings: a CPA
  • Whether the business model works at the new price, including margins and cash: an accountant or another financial professional

Peers can tell you how the conversation felt. They cannot tell you what your numbers should be.

the-founder-spouse-who-carries-the-compa.title: The spouse who carries the company with no title
the-founder-spouse-who-carries-the-compa.description: Their name is not on the cap table, but their life is. Peer notes on the founder's partner, at home or newly in Austin, and what founders say they do.
the-founder-spouse-who-carries-the-compa.html:
A founder at the IFN meetup table is explaining a hiring decision and mentions, almost in passing, that their partner is back home with the kids while they build here. The conversation moves on. Later, as people are packing up, someone asks a simple question: how is your partner doing? The founder starts to answer and then stops. They realize nobody has asked them that in months. They are not sure they have asked it themselves.

Some version of this comes up most months. This post is about the person whose name is not on the cap table but whose life is tied to it: the founder's spouse or partner. For international founders the setup is often split across two countries. One adult is in Austin and the other is still at home, or a partner moved here and set a career aside. This is peer orientation from the room. It is a different conversation from moving the whole family (the first 90 days post covers more of the arrival side).

Disclaimer

This is not relationship, legal, tax, immigration, or financial advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. What your partner and children are allowed to do here, how money and property work between you, and what your relationship needs all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

What the partner carries

Founders talk about runway as a company number. At home, it is often a household number. In many of the stories told in the room, the partner's salary is what keeps the rent paid while the founder draws little or nothing. Or the savings funding the first year were shared savings, and the partner agreed to spend them.

Then there is the work nobody invoices. School runs, sick days, the repair person, the bills. A partner who stayed home with children is often parenting alone for long stretches, on a calendar set by the founder's flights.

There is the explaining, too. Parents and in-laws ask when the company will make money, why the founder is still abroad, whether this was a good idea. The founder can answer from a distance. The partner is the one sitting at the family dinner.

Underneath it is the waiting. The founder gets feedback every day: a call went well, a customer left, an investor went quiet. The partner gets the summary, usually late, and has to decide how worried to be with less information than anyone.

The Balderton Founder Wellbeing Report 2024, a survey of 128 VC-backed founders, found 57% of married or partnered founders and CEOs reported a negative impact on their relationship. When it comes up in the room, people mostly recognize it.

Two versions of the same strain

The partner who stayed home. Time zones decide when you talk. The founder calls at the end of their day, which lands at the start of the partner's, or the reverse, and someone is always tired. Peers describe calls that slide into logistics: who paid what, which form the school needs back. Visits help. They also reset the clock on missing each other, and the goodbye at the airport does not get easier. The founder who is not there can miss how much solo parenting costs until a visit makes it visible.

The partner who moved. From outside, this version looks easier. The family is together. But the partner who moved has often paused a career, sometimes because of what their own status allows (a question for immigration counsel, not the room), sometimes because someone had to run the move. The founder lands in a city with a built-in reason to meet people: customers, investors, rooms like this one. The partner lands in the same city with none of that. Founders who have lived it say the loneliness on that side is easy to miss because it is quiet.

What peers say they do

This is not a program. It is what founders describe when they compare notes.

Tell them the real numbers. Founders who share the actual runway, the actual burn, and the actual pipeline say the conversations get calmer, even when the numbers are bad. A partner left guessing usually guesses worse.

Agree on how long, and what counts as enough. Some couples set a check-in point after which they sit down and decide again together. It might be a date, a revenue level, or a funding outcome. Then the decision belongs to both of them. The room does not suggest where that line should sit. That stays between the two of you.

Give them their own way in. A partner who moved to Austin needs people who are not there because of the founder. Some founders bring their partner to a meetup once and then step back. Others point them toward groups built around their partner's own field or interests. The first 50 connections post is written for founders, but much of it works for a partner starting from zero.

Say thank you, specifically. A general thank-you lands softer than naming the thing: the week of school runs while you were at a conference, the call with your parents they handled for you. Founders who started doing this say it costs nothing and they wish they had started sooner.

Some founders also say that talking with a couples counselor or licensed therapist, together or alone, helped them say things the weekly call could not hold. The room can point in that direction. It cannot do that work for you.

When we stop talking

The room can share how other founders handled the strain. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • Your spouse's or children's immigration status, including whether a partner can work here: immigration counsel
  • Money, savings, and property between partners, especially across two countries: a lawyer or a licensed financial professional
  • The relationship itself: a licensed counselor or therapist, together or on your own

If you or your partner are struggling day to day, a doctor or counselor is the right first call, before any peer group.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete question about the home side of founding: how another founder handles time zones with a partner at home, how they talked through runway with a spouse, or how a partner who moved found people of their own. Guests are welcome, and that can include your partner; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. The meetup happens at Station Austin. us-business-banking-document-pack.title: US business banking for international founders: what peers gather first
us-business-banking-document-pack.description: What international founders at IFN tend to gather before they walk into a US business banking conversation, at overview level.
us-business-banking-document-pack.html:
After formation and EIN talk, banking is the next wall at IFN Austin meetups. Founders often say they assumed the hard part was "being foreign." What they describe afterward sounds more like incomplete company paper: mismatched names, a registered-agent address used as the operating address, missing EIN confirmation, or ownership docs that do not match passport spellings.

This is peer orientation on what people tend to gather before they walk into a bank or remote onboarding flow. It is not a downloadable checklist, not a promise any bank will approve you, and not product endorsement. The fuller pack language belongs with membership and Resources.

Disclaimer

This is not banking, legal, tax, or immigration advice. Bank and fintech policies change. Underwriting is individual. Verify requirements with the institution you apply to. IFN shares patterns from founder conversations, not guarantees.

The wrong wall, in meetup language

A common story in the room: form a US LLC or C-corp from abroad, upload a passport and Articles PDF to a remote business account, get stalled or declined, then conclude "US banks do not want internationals."

Peers who cleared remote onboarding usually rewrite that story: the underwriter could not reconcile an incomplete company file. Nationality still matters for some products. Incomplete paper fails more often than founders expect.

Industry examples (not IFN endorsements): Mercury's How to open a U.S. bank account remotely and OtoCo's 2026 foreign-owned LLC banking guide. Your bank's checklist still wins.

What peers tend to gather (overview, not a pack)

Every institution differs. At a high level, founders who later cleared onboarding usually had these categories ready before they applied:

  • Formation evidence with the exact legal name, state, and filing date. Entity choice and sequencing are a separate peer conversation; keep company paper frozen before you apply.
  • EIN confirmation that matches that legal name. IRS EIN overview and Form SS-4 instructions.
  • Ownership and signing authority clear enough that beneficial owners and control persons are not a mid-review surprise.
  • Government IDs for owners and control persons, with names that match formation docs.
  • A real business mailing or principal place of business address, separate from the registered agent used only for service of process. Many remote underwriters reject registered-agent-only or PO box-only addresses. Check yours.
  • A boring, true business description. Vague activity language creates manual review. Inventing a safer-sounding industry creates a worse problem later.

That is orientation, not a fillable inventory. The item-by-item pack and member-channel walkthroughs live deeper in Resources and with membership.

Remote path vs traditional path

Remote path: browser upload plus review. Peers report stalls when the address is the registered agent, the EIN name mismatches, beneficial ownership is incomplete, or the activity is unsupported.

Traditional path: denser KYC, longer timelines, sometimes an in-person step. Branch visits with Articles alone often burn the trip.

Product names come and go. Re-read current eligibility pages, including any prohibited-residence list, before you build plans on a forum thread.

SSN, ITIN, and a separate visa track

In many remote stories, the company is the customer and controlling persons provide passport KYC. An SSN is not always required for the company account. An ITIN is personal; it is not a substitute for the company's EIN. Some banks still want a US person with signing authority.

Visa status is a separate track. Owning a US company is not permission to work in the United States. Keep personal status questions for immigration counsel, not for the banking underwriter.

When we stop talking

Call a professional or the bank's support channel when:

  • You need a product recommendation for your facts
  • Your industry or residence may be unsupported
  • Names or addresses already conflict across docs
  • Someone suggests misstating activity to pass review
  • Tax residency or payroll setup enters the chat
  • A decline letter needs interpretation against your KYC file

Meetup peers can share what they assembled. They cannot underwrite you.

Soft next steps

Bring your banking-prep questions (not your passport data) to the next IFN meetup. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check ifn.community. For the private member channel, members-only call, and the fuller banking pack / teaser PDF language as it ships, Become a member or browse Resources.

us-go-to-market-when-your-product-was-bu.title: US go-to-market when your first product was built elsewhere
us-go-to-market-when-your-product-was-bu.description: How pricing conversations, trust signals, and early channels change when a product built abroad starts selling to US buyers.
us-go-to-market-when-your-product-was-bu.html:
A founder sits at the IFN meetup table with an email thread open on their laptop. At home, the product sells through referrals and a short demo, and most deals close inside a few calls. Here, a US prospect liked the demo and then sent back a list of questions. Is there a security review document? Do you have a US entity? Can we talk to two US customers? What support hours do you keep in Central time? None of these came up at home. The founder wants to know which one to answer first, and whether the deal is even real.

The room hears some version of this most months. This post is peer orientation on what tends to change when a product built in one market starts selling into the US: how pricing conversations shift, which trust signals buyers look for, and which channels founders say worked first. It is not a go-to-market playbook, and it does not replace counsel or a CPA.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or financial advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Contract terms, privacy obligations, sales tax, and what your status allows you to do all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

Pricing conversations change shape

Founders rarely say their price was wrong. More often they say the way they presented it did not land.

US buyers, especially in B2B software, often expect clear packaging. That usually means a small number of tiers and a plain description of what each one includes. At home, a custom quote for every customer can work because relationships carry the sale. Here, it can feel like friction, or like a sign the product is not finished yet.

Annual versus monthly comes up a lot. Some buyers want monthly so they can try the product with less risk. Some finance teams prefer annual because it is easier to budget. Founders compare notes on which option they lead with and why. The room has no single answer. What peers suggest is deciding on purpose instead of copying the home model.

Currency gets less attention. If you quote in your home currency, or in a mix, the buyer has an extra step, and you can look like a vendor procurement has to set up specially. Most founders selling here end up quoting in US dollars. Then they have to work out how that money moves between the US entity and the team at home.

Sales tax is the one people find out about late. Depending on what you sell and where your buyers are, selling into US states can create obligations you did not plan for. The room raises the issue and stops there. It is CPA territory. For Texas specifically, the Texas Comptroller is the official place to start reading.

Trust signals US buyers ask for

When founders compare notes, the same requests come up across very different products.

A US entity and a US bank account. Procurement teams often want to pay a US company, into a US account, with a W-9 on file. A foreign entity can still close deals, but it adds questions at the worst point in the sale. Peers who sorted their banking early say it took one blocker out of every deal. The banking post covers what people gather first.

Contracts that look familiar to US buyers. If your agreement was drafted under home-country law with home-country conventions, the buyer's legal team may slow down or send back heavy redlines. Founders who had counsel review their customer terms for US buyers before they started selling say later deals moved faster. The room does not pass around contract language. That work belongs with a lawyer.

Support hours that overlap. Peers say round-the-clock coverage is rarely the ask. Buyers want to know which hours you cover in US time zones and what happens outside them. A buyer who knows you answer by mid-morning Central time is usually fine. A buyer who finds out by waiting is not.

References from US customers. Your first US customer counts for more than its revenue. Some founders ask early whether that customer would take a reference call later, and they keep the relationship warm so the answer stays yes. Logos from your home market still help, but many US buyers do not know them, so founders add a sentence of context.

A clear privacy and security posture. Security questionnaires show up earlier than most founders expect, sometimes before pricing does. Peers suggest having a plain description of how you handle customer data, where it is stored, and who can access it. Getting that description right for your product is a job for counsel. The FTC's business guidance is an official starting point for understanding how US regulators think about privacy and data security.

Say where the team is

Some founders admit they tried to look local at first: a US phone number, an Austin address on the website, and vague answers about where engineering sits. Most gave it up.

It usually comes out on the first scheduling call, when time zones show. A buyer who feels misled about something small starts to wonder what else is off. What works better is plain language: where the team is based, which hours you cover, and who the buyer's US contact is. Plenty of US buyers work with distributed teams every day. Surprises are what bother them.

Channels: what translated and what did not

Founders who got traction here describe a similar order, even if the timing varied.

Founder-led sales came first for nearly everyone. Early US conversations teach you what buyers misunderstand about your product, and you lose that if you hand sales off too soon. Warm intros came next. That is one reason people keep coming back to the meetup: someone in the room knows someone who buys what you sell. Niche communities in your industry, online and in person, often did more than general startup events. Partnerships with companies that already sell to your buyer helped some founders, though they usually took longer than expected.

Paid ads mostly came later. Founders who started with ads before they knew which message worked say they spent money and learned little.

On what translated from home, the answers are mixed:

  • Copy usually needed a rewrite. A straight translation rarely landed. Tone is often the gap: what reads as polite and thorough at home can read as slow or vague to a US buyer.
  • Spelling and formats matter more than people expect. British spelling, day-first dates, and metric-only specs tell a US reader the site was not written for them.
  • Case studies from home still carry weight when the problem is the same, but they need context a US reader can follow.
  • The core product usually traveled fine. What took the most work was the story around it.

When we stop talking

The room is useful for patterns. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • Customer contracts, terms of service, privacy policies, and data handling commitments: counsel who works with US commercial agreements
  • Sales tax, nexus, and revenue recognition for annual or multi-year contracts: a CPA, ideally one with cross-border experience
  • If you personally do sales, demos, or contract negotiation while you are in the US: immigration counsel, because what your status allows depends on your facts (the visa paths post covers where peer talk ends)

These are separate roles, and one professional rarely covers all of them.

Soft next steps

visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.title: Visa paths founders talk about at IFN (and when we stop talking)
visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.description: A peer map of visa paths founders discuss at IFN meetups, and the moments the room hands the conversation to immigration counsel.
visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.html:
Visa questions arrive early at IFN Austin meetups. Someone is still on a student timeline. Someone else is abroad and wondering whether to form a company first. Someone on an employer-sponsored status asks what they can do for a side project without putting their status at risk.

This is a peer orientation map of the paths that come up in the room. IFN does not file petitions. IFN does not tell you which visa you qualify for.

Disclaimer

This is not immigration, legal, tax, or banking advice. USCIS, the Department of State, and licensed immigration counsel are the authorities for eligibility, petitions, and status decisions. Rules change. Your facts matter. Use this only as meetup-shaped orientation, then verify with professionals and official pages before you act.

How the room talks about visas

Founders at IFN tend to talk in paths and constraints:

  • What status am I on now?
  • What am I allowed to do for a company I own?
  • What would a change of status or a consular application require?
  • Who petitions: me, my company, an employer, or a family member?
  • When do I stop brainstorming and hire counsel?

Peer stories help you ask better questions. They do not replace a case assessment. A careful public overview is Cooley's June 2025 note on foreign founders, visas, and corporate structure. Read it as orientation. Your attorney still owns your case.

The room also compares notes on timing: when to talk to counsel relative to incorporation, fundraising, or a planned trip. That timing talk stays peer pattern. It is never a filing calendar.

Paths that come up often (names + official links only)

The names below are classifications founders discuss at meetups. Official pages are linked so you can read primary language yourself. IFN does not score eligibility or assemble evidence packages.

  • O-1. Comes up when founders have a dense record of recognition in a defined field. The moment anyone asks "do I have enough evidence?" the room stops. USCIS O-1.
  • E-2. Comes up for nationals of qualifying treaty countries, usually alongside investment and ownership questions that are fact-specific. Check the treaty list first. USCIS E-2, Treaty Countries.
  • H-1B. Comes up around lottery calendars, employer-specific limits, and founder-owned company questions. IFN does not draw that line. USCIS H-1B.
  • L-1. Comes up when there is already a real foreign operating company, not only an idea. USCIS L-1A, L-1B.
  • Student and visitor timelines (F-1, OPT, B-1/B-2). Ownership and active work are different questions. As soon as the question becomes "am I allowed to do X on my current status?" the meetup conversation ends.
  • Green card / EB conversations. Peer orientation only. Counsel early. No eligibility theater.

Formation and visas are linked, but not the same project

A recurring IFN lesson: people form a US company and then assume the visa problem is solved. It is not.

Company paper and personal status move on different clocks. Peers who stay calm tend to keep a written list of what their current status allows, form the entity only when it serves a clear ops or fundraising job, gather banking materials after the entity exists, and book immigration counsel before they restructure equity "for a visa story."

When we stop talking

Call immigration counsel when:

  • You want a recommendation among O-1, E-2, H-1B, L-1, or any other path
  • You need evidence strategy, petition drafting, or consular prep
  • Your nationality, dual citizenship, or prior refusals change the map
  • You are on student or visitor status and want a green light for active work
  • Equity, board control, or vesting might be rearranged for status reasons
  • Someone offers you a "guaranteed" petition path in a group chat

IFN is a peer room. Counsel is a licensed professional with your facts and your file.

Soft next steps

Bring one status question to the next IFN meetup. Guests stay free via the meetup; register on Luma or see dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Deeper visa pathway maps and teaser PDFs live with membership and Resources as that hub fills in.

welcome-to-the-ifn-blog.html:
IFN runs a free monthly meetup in Austin for international and immigrant founders. The same questions show up every month: how people register a company in the United States, how they stay inside visa limits while they build, how they open a bank account, and how local funding conversations differ from the ones they had at home.

This blog is where we write those conversations down. Not legal advice. Not a course. Peer experience from founders who are doing the work in Austin, so you can arrive at the next meetup with sharper questions.

What you will find here

  • Field notes from the room: what surprised people who just landed, and what they wish they had asked earlier.
  • Orientation on visas, entity setup, banking, housing, hiring, and fundraising as an international founder, always as peer framing. When a topic needs counsel, we say so.

It is also not a newsletter signup page. When we publish, the post lives at /blog. Come to a meetup if you want the live version of the same conversation.

when-ai-takes-the-clients-who-used-to-pa.title: When AI takes the clients who used to pay your rent
when-ai-takes-the-clients-who-used-to-pa.description: The client did not leave for a cheaper agency. Peer notes from service owners on losing routine work to AI tools and what they are trying next.
when-ai-takes-the-clients-who-used-to-pa.html:
A founder who runs a small design and development studio sits down at the IFN meetup table and reads an email aloud from their phone. It comes from their best client, the one who has sent steady work for years. The tone is warm. The client thanks them for everything and says they will handle this kind of work in-house from now on. Someone asks who they hired. Nobody. In-house means a chat tool and a staff member who types requests into it. The table goes quiet for a moment. Then a few other people say something similar happened to them this year.

Some version of this comes up most months now. It usually comes from service owners and solo founders: designers, developers, writers, translators, and marketers who built a craft and then built a business around it. Many of them are immigrants who already rebuilt that craft once when they moved here. This post shares peer notes on what the loss feels like and what owners in the room say they are trying. It is not a tip sheet for using AI, and it is not financial or career advice.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, financial, or career advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Client contracts, intellectual property terms, and decisions about your business and income all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

What is leaving first

The client did not move to a cheaper agency. They opened a chat window, tried it on a task, and decided the result was close enough.

When owners look back at the work they lost, they often see the same pattern. The routine, repeatable work went first: the third version of a banner, the standard landing page, the first-draft translation, the monthly report that looked like last month's. That work was rarely the most interesting part of the business. It was often the part that paid the rent, because it came in every month without much selling.

Nobody at the table claims to know which jobs will disappear, and people who say they know are usually guessing. What owners can see is their own invoices. Many of them can point to the line items that have thinned out.

The Leapers 2025 report on UK freelancers found 33.2% said AI had already hurt their career. That survey covers the UK, and Austin is a different market. Still, the figure fits the mood in the room. People are not talking about some future risk. They are describing something that already happened to them.

What clients still pay for

When owners compare notes on the clients who stayed, the reasons sound alike across very different trades.

  • Judgment. Someone who looks at the draft and says it will confuse the buyer, or that it breaks something the client did not think about.
  • Accountability. A named person who owns the result and will still own it next month.
  • Taste. Knowing what good looks like for this client's customers, which a generated draft can only approximate.
  • Someone who answers when it breaks. The site goes down on a Friday, a campaign goes out with the wrong date, and the client wants a person on the phone.

Owners who kept their best relationships say those clients were rarely paying for output alone. They were paying for the person standing behind it.

The part people do not say out loud

This is the hardest part of the conversation, and the room tends to slow down for it.

There is grief. Some people spent years getting good at something, and now a client treats it as a commodity. That stings in a way that is hard to explain to anyone outside the trade. There is also fear, and it is usually concrete: rent, school fees, money sent home, a lease on a small office. Then there is embarrassment. Owners say they waited months before telling anyone, because losing a client to software felt like a personal failure instead of a market shift.

The immigrant angle comes up often. Many people in the room already rebuilt their craft once. They arrived with skills that did not translate directly, relearned how clients here buy, and built a reputation from nothing. Some say that history helps, because they know they have done it before. Others say it makes this harder, because they thought the rebuilding was over.

Peers can listen and share what they went through. If the weight of it starts to affect your sleep, your health, or how you get through the day, a doctor, therapist, or counselor is the right person to talk to.

What owners say they are trying

These are peer reports, not recommendations. Nobody at the table promises that any of them will work, and some owners tried one approach, dropped it, and moved to another.

Repackaging around outcomes. Some owners stopped selling hours or deliverables and started describing what the client gets: more qualified leads, a site that converts, a launch that goes out on time. They say it changed the conversation from "why should I pay you for this" to "can you get me there." How you present the offer matters as much as the work, a point the go-to-market post makes from a different angle.

Moving up to the part that needs a human. A few owners deliberately let the routine work go and focused on strategy, direction, review, and client relationships. That usually means fewer projects at a higher level. Several say the move took longer than they expected and left a thin stretch in between.

Using the tools themselves. Some owners use the same tools their clients tried and do more for the same client in the same time. They say the gain only lasts while their judgment is part of the package. If they ship whatever the tool produces, the client could have done that alone.

Finding buyers who want a person accountable. Some segments still want a named human responsible for the work, often because the stakes are high, the subject is regulated, or the buyer simply prefers it. Owners who went looking for those buyers describe it as a fresh validation exercise. The market validation post covers how people in the room test a new segment before committing to it.

Most owners who are getting through this are doing more than one of these at once, and they keep adjusting.

When we stop talking

The room is useful for patterns and for company. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • Contracts, intellectual property terms, and what you promise clients about AI use in your work, or what they can do with work you deliver: counsel who handles commercial agreements
  • Money decisions such as closing a line of business, cutting staff, taking on debt to bridge a gap, or restructuring how you pay yourself: a CPA or a licensed financial professional
  • Stress that follows you home and does not lift: a doctor, therapist, or counselor

These are separate roles, and one person rarely covers all of them.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete question about your service business: a client you think you are about to lose, an offer you are thinking about repackaging, or a segment you want to test. when-your-accent-or-foreign-degree-gets-.description: When an accent or a foreign credential lowers a US buyer's trust: peer notes on spotting the pattern, how foreign degrees are recognized, and what founders choose.
when-your-accent-or-foreign-degree-gets-.html:
A founder at the IFN meetup table has spent more than a decade building products at home. They have led teams, shipped launches and sold a company. Tonight they describe a sales call from last week. The buyer had been warm over email. A few minutes into the call, once the founder started walking through the demo, the questions got shorter, and no follow-up came. A few weeks before that, a potential partner asked twice where their degree was from, as if the first answer had not counted. Someone across the table nods. The first time it happened to them, they assumed the problem was their pitch and rewrote it more than once before they saw it differently.

The room hears some version of this most months. This post is peer orientation on what founders describe when an accent or a foreign credential seems to lower the trust a US buyer, partner or investor gives them. It covers how people tell a pattern from a bad fit, how foreign degree recognition works here, and what founders choose to do about it. Hiding who you are is not part of it. It is not legal, employment or immigration advice, and it does not replace counsel.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, employment, immigration, or professional licensing advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Whether a credential is accepted, whether treatment was unlawful, and what your status allows all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

What it looks like when it happens

Founders rarely describe one big moment. They describe small extra steps that add up.

One is the extra proof: a buyer asks for a second reference when a local vendor would only have needed one. Another is the meeting where the teammate or advisor who sounds local gets all the questions, even though you built the product. A third is a degree from a respected university at home that reads as unknown here, so the person across the table treats it as a blank line on your bio.

Peers are careful to separate a bad fit from a pattern. Sometimes a deal goes cold because the budget disappeared or the product did not match the need. Some calls go badly for everyone. What people watch for is repetition: the same kind of question, from the same kind of room, at the same point in the conversation. Founders who keep short, plain notes after calls say they see the picture more clearly over time than when they replay each call late at night.

Foreign degrees: who decides

This part has more structure than most people expect, though less than they would like.

The US has no single national body that recognizes foreign degrees. Whoever is asking decides. That might be an employer, a school or, for licensed professions, a state licensing board. Many of them ask for an evaluation from a private credential evaluation service, which compares your degree to a US equivalent. The US Department of Education has a page on recognition of foreign qualifications that explains how this works, and it is the official place to start reading. The room does not recommend particular evaluators. Which one fits depends on who is asking, so founders ask the requesting organization what it accepts.

Most founders selling a product never go through a formal evaluation. The degree comes up in a bio, a pitch deck or a partner's due diligence, and the real question is how much context to give. Some founders add a short line saying what the institution is and what the program covered. Others leave the degree out of sales materials and let the work carry the weight. If your field is a licensed profession, that is a separate question for the state licensing board where you want to practice.

What founders choose to do

Peers talk about these as choices. Different people make different ones, and the same person often changes their approach over time.

Many lead with proof a US buyer already knows how to read: shipped work, measurable results and references. A short case study with a clear outcome tends to settle doubts before anyone voices them. The go-to-market post covers the trust signals US buyers ask for in more depth.

Others bring in a US reference early. Founders who had one US customer, advisor or partner willing to vouch for them say later calls felt different. Some ask that person to join a first meeting with a new prospect.

Then there is the decision about when to name it. Some founders address it directly, with one sentence about where they built their career and what they did there. Others decide a particular meeting is not worth the energy and move on. Peers treat both as reasonable. What wears people down is deciding from scratch every single time, so some settle on a default and adjust from there.

The one that comes up most is the apology. Founders notice they open calls with "sorry, my English" and realize it frames everything that follows. Founders who stopped saying it say they felt different on calls, even when nothing else changed. The room does not trade accent-reduction tips. The accent belongs to the person who built the company.

The cost of carrying it

This part gets talked about less.

It looks like second-guessing a call afterward, rereading an email three times before sending it, or being the only person in the room who has to think about how they sound. It is a kind of tiredness that is hard to explain to people who have never had to carry it.

Part of why founders keep coming back to the meetup is that most people at the table have some version of the same story. You can skip the background and get straight to the question. Someone nearby has also been asked twice where their degree is from.

If the weight of it starts to follow you home, a licensed professional (a doctor, therapist or counselor) is the right person to talk to. Peers can listen, but they cannot do that job.

When it goes further

Some situations go well past a cold sales call. If treatment in hiring or employment, yours or your team's, starts to look like discrimination based on where someone is from, there are official channels. The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has a page on national origin discrimination that explains the federal side. The room does not try to decide whether something counts. That is a question for employment counsel, and the legal counsel post covers how founders find the right kind of lawyer.

When we stop talking

The room is good for recognizing patterns and comparing choices. Bring in professional help when any of these come up:

  • Whether treatment in hiring or employment was unlawful discrimination: employment counsel, with the EEOC for the federal process
  • Whether a foreign qualification lets you practice a licensed profession: the state licensing board for that profession in that state
  • Anything about your immigration status, including what work you can do while you are here: immigration counsel

These are separate roles, and one professional rarely covers all of them.

working-the-austin-day-and-the-home-coun.title: Working the Austin day and the home-country night
working-the-austin-day-and-the-home-coun.description: Your workday runs on Central Time and the people at home live on another clock. Peer notes on family calls, guilt and the habits founders keep across time zones.
working-the-austin-day-and-the-home-coun.html:
A founder at the IFN meetup table says they took their mother's call at five in the morning. It was the only window before her evening ended. At nine they ran a customer meeting, and the customer had no idea the founder had already been up for hours. Around midnight they were answering the family group chat, because that was when everyone at home was having breakfast and sending photos. Nobody planned the day that way. It became the day, and then it became most days.

The room hears some version of this most months. This post is peer orientation on the part of founder life that sits outside the company: staying close to family when your workday runs on Central Time and the people you answer to at home live on a different clock. It covers what founders say gets squeezed and what they have tried. It is not a productivity system, and it does not replace a doctor, counsel, or a CPA.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, medical, or financial advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Health, travel, status, and money sent across borders all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

The shape of the double day

Most founders describe two days stacked on top of each other. The Austin one has customers and a calendar. The home one has no calendar at all, which is part of why it spreads.

It usually starts before dawn. A parent calls early because that is a reasonable hour on their side, and you pick up because missing it means waiting another day. Then the Austin day runs as normal. Late at night the phone lights up again: the group chat, a sibling with news, a question about a form your father needs help with.

Birthdays are the ones people mention most. A child turns a year older or a parent marks a milestone, and the founder is on a sales call when the cake comes out. They watch the video afterward, between meetings.

Then there is the call that comes at the wrong hour. A parent's health worry, a test result, a hospital visit. It tends to land in the middle of the night or in the middle of an investor update, and neither is a good time. Some founders say this is when the distance stops feeling abstract.

What gets lost

Sleep is the obvious one, and founders say so plainly. They also describe two quieter losses.

The first is presence with the people who are actually in Austin. That might be a partner who moved with you, or new friends from the meetup. If your mornings and nights belong to home, the people here get the tired middle of the day, or nothing. A founder who spends every evening on the phone with home can go months without really arriving in Austin. The first 90 days post touches on what helps people settle.

The second is harder to name. Some founders describe it as never quite being in one place. Your body is in Austin, your attention keeps checking on a city many hours away, and you are a little behind in both. People say it makes small decisions feel heavier than they should.

If your sleep or your health is suffering, talk to a doctor. That is the plain answer, and the room will tell you the same.

What peers say they set up

Nobody in the room has a system, and the ones who tried to build one usually dropped it. What comes up instead is a handful of habits that seem to hold.

A fixed family call slot that both sides protect. One time, on set days, that works at both ends. Founders say protecting it matters more than which slot you pick. That means not booking a customer call over it, and asking family to hold it too instead of calling whenever something comes up. Some keep it short on weekdays and longer on weekends.

Telling family when you are actually reachable. It sounds obvious, and people skip it anyway. Parents may not know what your day looks like here, or they assume you are free because you used to be. Founders who sent a plain message ("I am in meetings during these hours, I will call back after") say it eased a lot of quiet worry on the other side. Family stopped reading a missed call as bad news.

Letting some messages wait until morning. Not every group chat message needs an answer at midnight. Some founders mute the chat at night and let calls from a few people ring through, so a real emergency still reaches them. Others agree with family on one line that means "call me now."

One longer visit a year, planned early. Short trips home squeezed between fundraising and launches tend to leave everyone feeling shortchanged. Founders who block one longer visit well ahead say family has something to look forward to, and the business can plan around it. If travel touches your status, take that question to immigration counsel before you book.

One practical thing catches people out. Daylight saving time does not change on the same dates everywhere, and some countries do not change their clocks at all. For a stretch each spring and fall, the family slot can drift by an hour, and someone ends up waiting on a call that comes at the wrong time. Founders who have been caught by it now check the dates for both places and send a reminder home ahead of time.

The guilt runs both ways

This is the part of the conversation where the table tends to go quiet.

Founders feel guilty toward home for not being there: the missed birthday, or the sibling carrying more of a parent's day-to-day care. They also feel guilty toward the people here, and toward the company, for being half-present while they answer home. Some carry both at once and assume everyone else has it worked out.

What peers describe is a point where they decide on purpose what they will carry and what they will not. That might mean accepting that a sibling at home handles daily care while you take on a set share of something else. It might mean saying out loud that you will miss some events and be fully there for others. People say the guilt stays, but it sits differently once it is a choice they made.

Talking it through with other founders who live with the same clock helps more than people expect. The first 50 connections post covers how people find those conversations early.

When we stop talking

The room is useful for patterns and for company. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • Your own health, including sleep: a doctor
  • Caring for a parent from abroad, including medical decisions or paperwork on their behalf: their doctors and care professionals where they live, and a lawyer in that country if decisions need formal authority
  • Travel plans, time spent outside the US, and what your status allows: immigration counsel
  • Money you send home regularly and how it is treated on either side: a CPA, ideally one with cross-border experience

These are separate roles, and one professional rarely covers all of them.
